As intelligence becomes too cheap to meter, then the big opportunity is driving diffusion of AI into the economy. 

This is a great time to be applied AI company because there’s an incredible amount of innovation and competition acting as a tailwind to your own progress. Huge moment for startups right now that can take advantage of this.

How to build great evals - part 5

Stop dumbing down the results from your beaut…
items.summaryText:
How to build great evals - part 5

Stop dumbing down the results from your beautiful, complex eval suite into one single score. This often happens because some senior wants a simplified number to make decisions. Happened to us in the early days of Gemini.

And I see it happening with a lot of teams.

This is the tyranny of the average.
AI systems do not have a simple dimension of quality.

Imagine a model that goes from:
85% -> 89% on simple summarization
80% -> 85% on basic factual QA
70% -> 63% on complex financial analysis

A single score obscures the fact that the model got worse on your frontier use case.

The immediate reaction to this is to come up with a weighted score. The problem with this is that you have  created false, mathematical procession around a judgment call.

So what should you do?
- keep a prioritized list of your evals per the ladder we discussed in part 4 yesterday.
- get people who can look at the details and don’t look for abstracted simplicity.
- Understand all the critical eval results in depth, where they fail, where they shine and make a decision on whether your new AI system is better or worse for your users.

Next post tomorrow!

Drop your eval questions below and I will answer in future posts.

Share this with your teammates. And your managers who run from complexity.

items.summaryZh:
如何构建出色的评估——第5部分

不要把你漂亮而复杂的评估套件的结果简化为一个单一分数。这通常是因为某位高管想要一个简化的数字来做决策。我们在 Gemini 早期就遇到过这种情况。

而且我看到很多团队都在发生同样的事。

这就是平均值的暴政。
AI 系统并没有单一的质量维度。

想象一个模型从：
简单摘要任务 85% -> 89%
基础事实问答 80% -> 85%
复杂财务分析 70% -> 63%

一个单一分数会掩盖模型在最前沿用例上变差的事实。

对此的第一反应是提出一个加权分数。问题在于，你围绕一个主观判断制造了一种虚假的数学推演。

那么你该怎么做？
- 按照我们昨天在第4部分讨论的阶梯，维护一份优先级排序的评估列表。
- 让那些能够看到细节、不追求抽象简化的人参与。
- 深入理解所有关键评估结果，了解它们在哪里失败、在哪里发光，然后判断你的新 AI 系统对用户来说是更好还是更差。

明天发下一篇！

在下面留下你的评估问题，我会在未来的文章中回答。

把这分享给你的队友，以及那些逃避复杂性的管理者。

I think I'll use Instinct more as an assistant for random chores and tasks.

items.bodyText:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:24
COVID happened, Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, and we're like, oh, this might just be a flash in the pan, like treadmills and sourdough bread. But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the mittens bot and the cheating scandal. And we just spiked again. And then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline.

Speaker 2 | 00:24 - 00:29
How do you think about, like, how to design a rating system for poker?

Speaker 1 | 00:29 - 00:48
We're bringing the chess playbook, which is like, how good are you really? Not just can you buy the most chips or can you use a bot or can you steal the most money? Whatever it is, we've all played those games where you're playing for M and M's and someone's just, like, all in all the time and they just rebuy more M and M's. As people get used to, like, wait. I actually care about my poker rating.

Speaker 1 | 00:48 - 00:57
People are gonna care about it as much as money because it's a reflection of, like, the value and their skill as a player. I think this is gonna be quite an interesting innovation for for

Speaker 2 | 01:10 - 01:44
the chess.com domain out of bankruptcy auction in 2005 for $55 when almost every investor told him it was an uninvestable niche passion project. Two decades later, he's built the dominant chess platform with more than 250,000,000 members, 200,000,000 a year in revenue and a mission to get a billion people to play chess. It's a game that's more popular than ever, despite computers outclassing humans at it for the last thirty years. We talk about what AI means for games, the future of chess.com, how to build a rating system for poker and the future of human skills. Welcome, Eric.

Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:47
Eric, it's great to have you on No Priors. Welcome.

Speaker 1 | 01:47 - 01:49
Thank you so much for having me.

Speaker 2 | 01:49 - 02:05
So I'd love to just make sure our listeners have a little bit of the backstory of chess.com and how you built this business. But could you paint a little bit of a picture of just, you know, usage and both the company and the user base and product today first?

Speaker 1 | 02:05 - 02:25
Yeah, sure. We are we are much larger than I ever thought we would be. So it's kind of wild to say these numbers for me. We're about 10,000,000 daily active users, about 40 or 50,000,000 monthly active users. It's always a little slower in the summertime as people are, you know, in the, in the Northern Hemisphere out and about.

Speaker 1 | 02:26 - 02:55
We have more than two fifty million registered members and more revenue than I thought we would end up with as a chess company. A little, I think this year we'll do a little over 200,000,000, which is frankly, again, surprising. We have about six fifty people on our team who love chess, are passionate about the game, and are working hard to, you know, make our members happy and to grow the game, and to be the best possible place to work. Those are our three kind of the three areas of our mission.

Speaker 2 | 02:55 - 03:10
Amazing. And you took a, I guess, somewhat unconventional startup path or founder CEO path to get here. I'm certainly think of you as founder. What how did you end up owning the business?

Speaker 1 | 03:11 - 03:41
Well, we didn't start by owning a business. We just started by owning a domain name that we got from a bankruptcy auction in 2005. Someone else owned the domain name. They were building chess software, but they, you know, couldn't pay their, their debts and, and the money they'd raised a little bit of money to try to do that, and ended up with a failed business. And so, a friend and I bought the chess.com domain name for $56,000 and we were going to build a chess community.

Speaker 1 | 03:41 - 03:53
We wanted to be like MySpace and build a chess community where people could kind of come and, and and express themselves and learn and share. We bought the domain name and started building.

Speaker 2 | 03:53 - 04:00
And, we'll bridge the gap from that to the scale of community you have today. Like, how did you grow? How did you think about fundraising?

Speaker 1 | 04:01 - 04:16
Yeah. So, did think about fundraising. You know, obviously, I was at, I was at Stanford Business School at the time. So, you know, Sandhill Road was right there, and I had access to a lot of venture capitalists. They were, you know, teachers and guests in, you know, classrooms I was in.

Speaker 1 | 04:16 - 04:29
And so I had a lot of meetings and basically most of them said, this is uninvestable. You should get a real job. Don't waste your time with this. And so I wasn't able to raise any money. No one believed in the vision.

Speaker 1 | 04:29 - 04:42
I asked some classmates if they wanted to like join me on this venture. And they're like, nah, we're going go like do something serious. And, so then my friend and I, you know, he was kind of the CTO. I was the product person. Just the two of us started building it together.

Speaker 1 | 04:43 - 05:31
Didn't raise any money. Eventually I started putting money in. I had money from a, you know, a couple of previous businesses I had sold, borrowed like a little bit of money from my friend's mom, and then paid it back later, but, you know, we just really kind of grew at the speed of cash, and after we launched in 2007, right as I graduated, from school, and then I think within like eighteen months, we were starting to charge memberships for like online chess learning, and we pretty quickly became profitable, and then we just grew, you know, as we had more revenue, we would just hire somebody new, whether it was a community manager, a developer, a system, a SIS admin, you know, eventually designers. It just kind of grew as we had money to, you know, for it to grow. And we never then again considered raising money.

Speaker 1 | 05:31 - 05:46
It never crossed our minds. We just thought, Hey, we're profitable. Let's just keep, let's keep growing. And we always thought like, oh, when we hit like 50 people, like we're never going to have more than 50 people on our team. And of course we blew, we're never going to have more than a 100 people on our team.

Speaker 1 | 05:46 - 06:18
And then we just stopped saying that because, you know, chess just continued to surprise us as to how big it got. And it still surprises me. But what's interesting is now I'm like, if two fifty million people have said they want to play chess at some point on chess.com, like, why don't we have 50,000,000 daily active users? You know, a billion people should be playing chess. So now our ambitions are pretty big and we see the good that chess does in the world and brings people together and gives them confidence and, you know, teaches them that you never really lose if you learn.

Speaker 1 | 06:18 - 06:29
And it's a great game for learning and spending time. So now our mission is huge and we're like, we're going to be, you know, bigger than we are today. So we're quite excited about our mission.

Speaker 2 | 06:29 - 06:45
How did you think about competition and like the rate of growth you needed to have? Yeah. And how do you think about it today? Because there there are I don't know if you can say the words, but there are platforms like Leechess out there. Yeah.

Speaker 2 | 06:46 - 07:05
Amongst the many drivers of people raising a huge amount of capital, some businesses are more CapEx intensive than others. But even when they're not naturally. The desire to like be the dominant player in a market, way chess.com is right is, I think, a common driver.

Speaker 1 | 07:05 - 07:22
Yeah, and I think that's fair. And I want to give the caveat that the chess, you know, the chess industry, as we call it today, didn't exist, you know, twenty years ago. It was like some some apps and like one kind of, you know, a couple of players. There was free Internet chess server fix. There was ICC Chess Club.

Speaker 1 | 07:23 - 07:33
Those were the two major players. There's Yahoo! Chess. And, you know, we came on and we just relentlessly focused on what we wanted as players ourselves. We wanted a product that felt great.

Speaker 1 | 07:33 - 07:44
We wanted it to be free to play. We wanted it to be in the browser. We wanted it to feel great. You know, we wanted it to be a wonderful experience. So, we really just focused on the user experience above all.

Speaker 1 | 07:44 - 07:59
And, you know, over time, you know, that wins out. And so, you know, most of the others kind of fell by the wayside. Obviously, Leechess exists today. They're kind of the, I would say, the Linux of, you know, they exist for a really important reason. It's great for the community.

Speaker 1 | 07:59 - 08:24
It's open source. It does what it does. And we coexist here and, you know, we drive the growth of the game through what we do and, you know, through the investments we're allowed to, we're able to make due to the fact that we do generate revenue, and, you know, they serve a different part of it. The interesting thing is chess is like not patentable. There's, you know, thousands, if not tens of thousands of chess apps in the App Store and chess websites.

Speaker 1 | 08:24 - 09:06
And, you know, at the end of the day, really, is going to win out and community and content. And so it's just really this this relentless focus on creating the best possible experience. I do think there's other markets and businesses where you need to to raise money, whether to move at speed. Again, we've built this for twenty years, so others need to move faster or more at speed or there's more investment in certain areas or obviously if there's hardware or inventory, those are different types of businesses. But for a pure software and content business like ours, you know, and one where we didn't have, like, you know, no major tech company was bearing down on us, we were able to kind of take a little bit of the slower, a slower road there, which was great.

Speaker 1 | 09:06 - 09:11
It developed a great culture and allowed us to, you know, not not need outside capital.

Speaker 2 | 09:12 - 09:39
So you said that part of why you were able to grow in the way you did was there were not a lot of people who believed that, you know, the business would be as big as it is or the industry would actually be an industry. At what point? I was it a progressive thing? At what point did you think like, oh, this is actually going to be a big business versus, you know, it's something I'm personally passionate about?

Speaker 1 | 09:40 - 09:47
Yeah, I think 2024 was when we thought this would be a big business.

Speaker 2 | 09:47 - 09:48
That was not that long ago.

Speaker 1 | 09:48 - 10:23
Long ago. Because before before COVID and Queen's Gambit, we had like a million daily active users, and we were shocked at that. And but then when COVID and Queen's COVID happened, Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, we're and like, oh, this might just be a flash in the pan, like treadmills and sourdough bread and other things that people did during, you know, COVID. And we might just come back down to where we were. But we actually stayed really high after that, a little bit lower than our peak in 2022.

Speaker 1 | 10:23 - 10:55
But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the mittens bot and the cheating scandal and all these other things in 2023, and we just spiked again. And then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline. And so kind of in 2024, we're like, oh my gosh, like this thing is actually sticking around. It's actually growing and compounding over time. I think this is a lot bigger than we thought it was going to be, which was, you know, fascinating.

Speaker 1 | 10:55 - 11:22
It's also terrifying, in some ways because, you know, it's always like if your business is shrinking, it's scary because how do you make it grow? If your business is flat, it's scary because, you know, how do you make it grow? If your business is going up, it's scary because like how do you maintain that growth or how do you deal with it? You know, we were like literally just like, you know, we had issues with scalability across the product and the tech and all those things. And so it's been pretty white knuckle.

Speaker 1 | 11:22 - 11:49
I think for the last year, it's actually been more calm than it ever has been just because we've had the team in place and, you know, our growth is more predictable. And we finally kind of gotten our hands around ally what it means to be a 650 person fully remote company. So it's been pretty it's been pretty smooth, and we're now focused on a lot of experimentation and product improvements and, you know, infrastructure and tech and obviously the integration of A. I. And what that's meaning.

Speaker 1 | 11:49 - 11:53
And so it's been an interesting last twelve months for sure.

Speaker 2 | 11:53 - 12:11
I want to ask about two more business topics and then talk about A. I. In the context of chess and sort of your your reflections on that. And the first would just be how do you like? The Queen's Gambit and sort of the, you know, increasing cultural relevance of chess.

Speaker 2 | 12:11 - 12:13
Like, what's your what's your reflection of that?

Speaker 1 | 12:14 - 12:33
Yeah. Honestly, it's like it's incredible because when I was, you know, I got into chess a little bit late in life. I was 18, you know, so going to college and getting into the game, and I'm like, nobody plays chess. No one talks about chess. Like, it's almost like a secret hobby.

Speaker 1 | 12:33 - 12:45
You know? I was kind of I was kind of like a skater snowboarder who, like, kept chess as, like, the secret thing I did. You know, when I was in high school, was like for nerds. No one would talk about it. Like, would you why would you spend time on that?

Speaker 1 | 12:46 - 13:17
So that's what I grew up with. And then now to have my own kids where, you know, all their friends are playing chess and like chess is cool and like the jocks play chess and the nerds play chess and like everybody plays chess. And then you've got like, you know, Louis Vuitton centers their whole, you know, fashion shoot around chess. And like, it just blows my mind. It's like, you know, and I do feel partly just along for that ride, but I also feel that we've been partly responsible for that, we've kind of revolutionized what it means to be a chess player.

Speaker 1 | 13:17 - 13:37
Chess can be in your pocket. You can do it any time. The content is funny and relevant and interesting. And we also just redefined what it meant to be a chess player because previously, you know, it was like you weren't really a chess player until you were 2,000 or above, right, rated. If you weren't that, you weren't really there and you didn't, you weren't really a chess player.

Speaker 1 | 13:37 - 14:05
But now everybody, you know, we kind of change the narrative and we celebrate your mistakes and when you hang your queen and when you, you know, if you're rated 500, that's fine. You're still a chess player. You're still part of the community and you're on your journey. So I think that, like, it's been like honestly one of the great honors of my life to be a part of that and to see that we kind of culturally change what what it means. And, you know, when you see pictures of, like, Lewis Hamilton, like, flying in his private jet, playing chess on his phone, it's just like it blow it blows my mind.

Speaker 1 | 14:05 - 14:07
So, it's it's been wild.

Speaker 2 | 14:07 - 14:19
Yes. Yes. I was the, you know, high school nerd that played chess. But my my kids now are eight year old plays and teaches chess. And it's like very common.

Speaker 2 | 14:19 - 14:47
They're in a nerdy town, but it's it's like common enough that, you know, I don't know, 20% of the kids do after school chess, right? Which is a totally wild thing to think about soccer. Seriously. You had a huge announcement recently, and that's a big change in terms of the CBC investment. Tell us about that, what it means to the business, how you thought about working with a private equity firm after so many years of just, you know, being a bootstrapped business.

Speaker 1 | 14:47 - 15:19
Yeah. Well, I'll tell you, we're still a bootstrapped business because CVC came in, but they still, you know, they, they, they came in and bought secondary. That was part of the fundraising cycle. Obviously, General Atlantic was the really the first private equity to believe in us. You know, back in 2020 or 2021, you know, they saw our growing business and they had conviction that we, you know, we're a strong player in an interesting market, and they came in and, you know, we had another investor.

Speaker 1 | 15:19 - 15:36
You know, it's kind of interesting because if you go back in time, like, we were just this privately, entirely privately held, and then, you know, someone comes along and is like, Oh, I love chess. I want to invest. And we're like, No, no, no. And then finally we said yes, and they bought like a little bit. And they're like, I'll hold on to this forever.

Speaker 1 | 15:36 - 15:42
I just want to be a part of this. And then like five years later, like, I need to get out of this. I need to sell. What? You said you were going to be here forever.

Speaker 1 | 15:42 - 15:54
Like, don't worry, I got another guy. So then this other investor came in. He's like, no, but I want to own X% and like we're like reluctantly let him a little bit more in. And he's like, but I love chess. I'll be here forever.

Speaker 1 | 15:54 - 16:18
And then, you know, three years later, he's like, I got to sell. What? You said you're going be here. So then we were at such a scale that like we had to like find a different scale of investor. And so we did the rounds with all the private equity and, you know, really just did not enjoy that process and really didn't enjoy most of the people that I met during that time, you know, really were focused on, I thought, the wrong things.

Speaker 1 | 16:18 - 16:48
But when I met, you know, General Atlantic and Tanzan there, you know, they really believed in our mission, and they believed that if we focused on our mission, that we would build a wonderful business. And that was that aligned with with what we felt. And so they made an investment, but again, secondary buying shares from existing investors, no infusion of capital. And then eventually they came to their fundraising cycle times. You know, they've got to return, you know, make returns to partners and do their do their thing.

Speaker 1 | 16:48 - 17:19
And so then we, again, had to now look for another person to come in, and we found CVC. We were we were very, very happy, to be working with CVC. They have such a deep experience in gaming, in sports, in community businesses, and we really just felt like a bond and an alignment that like when you take care of your community and your product, that you'll build a great business. So, they invested in, buying out different shares from different people. The General Atlantic reinvested as well.

Speaker 1 | 17:19 - 17:34
So they're, they're still with us, in, in the new venture together, and, we're as committed as ever to continue to grow the game and to, and to follow our mission. But yeah, we're still, no, no, no capital needed to grow this business.

Speaker 2 | 17:34 - 17:40
How does it change? Has it changed the way you run the business? Do you have these increasingly at scale outside investors?

Speaker 1 | 17:41 - 17:44
Yeah, it actually has. But in a in a wonderful way.

Speaker 2 | 17:44 - 17:51
Okay, this is like, you know, against the conventional wisdom of like private equity being involved. So say more.

Speaker 1 | 17:51 - 18:18
Yeah, I can recognize that like a lot. You know, you kind of hear the tropes about private equity and, you know, where they where they give you money and then just say work harder or whatever, do better. It hasn't been like that at all with General Atlantic or any of our with CVC at all. Really, it's it's great knowledge sharing across what they've seen in the industry and what we do. They're in the weeds on the product and the community, and they've really been great at pushing us to be our best.

Speaker 1 | 18:18 - 18:39
Not just saying, you know, do better, but like, here's some areas. Have you looked at this? And it's all it's just made us stronger. And then all the operational stuff, all the forecasting and all the kind of operational excellence that we've really brought to bear that we've needed to do to kind of grow up and do this. It's been wonderful and has made us better and stronger.

Speaker 1 | 18:39 - 19:13
And as our reporting gets better, we learn more about things and, you know, we experiment and we learn and all those things like really matter, not just for reporting to investors, but actually operating the business. So, yeah, I actually have really enjoyed our time with General Atlantic. Made it made us great. I've learned so much as a CEO, you know, being a being an entrepreneur, you know, with with two to five other people on your team or 10, that's that's one thing. But being the CEO of like a, you know, you know, many hundreds of people and, you know, many billions of valuations or whatever, like it changes the landscape of what I do.

Speaker 1 | 19:14 - 19:29
I'm just grateful that they've been there to help kind of help me learn to grow into these different roles. And, you know, that has kind of progressed along my own path as we, you know, as I lead this company. And so we've matured a lot, and it's been great.

Speaker 2 | 19:30 - 20:04
Super cool. One of the reasons I was excited to talk to you besides being excited about chess was that chess is probably our longest running experiment. And what happens to a human activity after the machines become like superhuman at it? Because it's been like what Deep Blue was thirty years ago, right? You know, we were just talking about how there are different drivers and it could be cultural orientation of the community, could be tools, it could be moments and content like Queen's Gambit.

Speaker 2 | 20:04 - 20:20
But the answer is humans definitely care more about chess than they did thirty years ago. Right? I think there are a lot of predictions when Deep Blue beat Kasparov that like chess was over. Right? Like, what did what did people misunderstand about why humans play games or what do you think happened instead?

Speaker 1 | 20:20 - 20:33
Yeah, it's it's so it's so interesting. You know, fundamentally, humans want to do human stuff. That's, you know, humans competing against other humans. It's humans making things. It's humans solving problems.

Speaker 1 | 20:33 - 21:23
And there are certain areas where, you know, machines have gotten better than humans at things, but it really, in the case of chess, pushed humans to be better and to do better in their field. And it's really interesting because, you know, grandmasters and world champions were using early versions of computers to kind of help them with ideas that they would then take into the human versus human realm. And then at some point the computers got so much better, and there was like Stockfish, as this kind of chess engine it was called, And that chess computer, like, actually made chess pretty boring for a little while because it was so perfect. All these players tried to play like the best computer. They were like grinding out these boring end games and it like kind of just got boring.

Speaker 1 | 21:24 - 22:26
But then neural nets came along, and so that was the next iteration of AI, which is like, you know, where early in the game of Go with, you know, you know, Leela and these neural nets came along and they started training chess on different chess positions and they let this self reinforcing learning come out And they ended up with Leela Chess Zero, the chess engine, and that started beating Stockfish in ways that was like unexpected. And it was actually aggressive and it did like unconventional things and like really push the game forward. And so what was interesting is that like computers at first made chess a little bit more boring, but then made it so much more exciting. And we're seeing more exciting chess than we ever have. And the players have gotten better and really computers are now able to help us unlock the game in ways that like make our enjoyment of the game better, whether it's the AI kind of coach on game review that reviews your game and helps you learn from it, or playing against the computer or generating puzzles that are, you know, specific for you.

Speaker 1 | 22:26 - 22:41
So AI has just really helped, you know, humans enjoy chess more. I don't know exactly how that's going to play out. I know that right now, like AI and mathematics is a big deal. Like, is it solving too many problems? But then you've got AI that's like unfolding proteins and solving for cancer.

Speaker 1 | 22:42 - 22:58
But, you know, humans are doing the research too. So it's really this kind of like hand in hand partnership where like the best of human creativity, the best of AI can help move humans further. So I don't know. I'm pretty I'm pretty optimistic about the future, honestly.

Speaker 2 | 22:58 - 23:18
I'm very inspired by the idea that AI can help humans get better at things much faster than they used to or technology in general. Like if you took a talented 10 year old today versus thirty years ago, like how much faster do you think they could reach? Elo 2,000 or master or something.

Speaker 1 | 23:18 - 24:05
I mean, we're seeing it already, like there's just younger and younger players or seven year olds who are giving a, you know, a run to grandmasters and, you know, 10 year old, I'm going butcher her name, so I'm not even going to say it, but from India, from England, she's crushing everybody. She's incredible. And to your point, like take the 10 year old and give them the tools and see where they come out. Like, when my son was, you know, younger than 10, you know, he obviously had access to YouTube and he had access to different things. And now he's 18 years old and, you know, he is is a better video game creator than, you know, I ever would have been because he self learned everything on YouTube and with, you know, different AI tools and with, you know, he doesn't use AI in the creative side, but he but he uses it for research on how to solve problems.

Speaker 1 | 24:06 - 24:41
And so this access to information, this access to, you know, you know, superhuman intelligence really is making people learn faster and better. And so to your point, like who knows what's going to be coming next in the in the next generation for those who, you know, are young now as they learn faster, what what can what will they create? I think the downside and the scare that everybody has is like, well, when there's a super intelligent, you know, AI that knows everything, like, why would anyone ever write an essay ever again? Like, why would they ever think? Why would they ever do anything?

Speaker 1 | 24:41 - 25:09
If you can just AI say, you know, draw me a picture of, you know, X, Y, Z thing, why would a human ever do it? And I understand that point of view. I have my worries. I think there's research that shows that people who use AI, like in certain areas, like do stop thinking and engaging their brain, but so we have to set up guardrails. We're going to have to figure out what works and what doesn't, but again, I think it's going to it's going to push people further into learning and creating better things.

Speaker 2 | 25:09 - 25:23
If everyone has this information access that you describe, like, why aren't we all equally good at chess? Right? Like, you know, what is what is having access to this due to the skill distribution in your data or in your experience?

Speaker 1 | 25:24 - 26:04
I mean, like anything, you know, you've got to do the repetitions to put it in your brain, you know, just because we have access So to it. It's really about people putting in a little bit of work. And one thing that I really love is the concept that if you just take any given day in your life and multiply that by a thousand, that's kind of what your life looks like. So if you do five chess puzzles a day, multiply that by a thousand, you've done 5,000 chess puzzles, you're going to be much better, right? Now that if you want to do a 100 puzzles a day, multiply that by a thousand, right?

Speaker 1 | 26:04 - 26:28
Or play 10 chess games a day or do yoga every day for ten thousand years, it's ten thousand days or a thousand days. It's not the actual individual one thing that you do on one day, but it's your habits that really compound over time. You can put that into any field, right? Whether, you know, you do one sketch a day or you, you know, go for one small run every day. And it's the same in any field, right?

Speaker 1 | 26:28 - 27:05
If you do research into any topic. And that's one thing that I do think AI is so great at is like you can literally get into, you know, whatever AI program you're using and you can start researching something and it can walk you through and it can help you get exposure to ideas, refine ideas, you know, get it. You can walk through and have these conversations and access to like walking into a professor's office and, you know, starting to ask questions. But you get it in your pocket all the time.
